Examples:
  nyx setup
  nyx setup --config ./nyx.yaml
  nyx setup --update-threat-data

setup opens a full-screen editor for the config file: your API keys (each can be tested without being
saved), the output directory and the common settings, the stages to skip, and a tab for the threat data nyx
checks addresses against. Edits to the config file are held until you save. It needs a terminal and takes no
arguments. The config file is where every setting and key nyx uses is kept.

setup --update-threat-data is its one use without the editor (u on the Threat data tab runs the same update):
it downloads Spamhaus's DROP lists and ipapi.is's abuse lists, needs no terminal, reads no config file and
exits. It writes the downloaded copy, and nothing else, to the threat-data directory beside the default
config file: spamhaus.jsonl and ipapi.json, each with a state file and a lock file. Its exit codes are 0 when
no source failed, 7 when one did, 1 when both did, 2 when there is nowhere to keep the data, and 130, 143 or
129 on a signal.

Usage:
  nyx setup [flags]

Flags:
      --config string        Config file (default $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/nyx/config.yaml, else ~/.config/nyx/config.yaml)
      --update-threat-data   Update the threat data (Spamhaus's DROP lists and ipapi.is's abuse lists) and exit, with no editor, no terminal and no config file
  -h, --help                 Help for setup

Shared flags:
      --debug   Also write diagnostics to stderr: each failed check (recon), each request to the NVD (cve), each address probed (ip --active), and the stack of an unexpected failure
  -J, --json    Print the result as one JSON object on stdout, and any error as one JSON line on stderr
  -q, --quiet   Write only warnings and errors to stderr; recon's summary is still printed

Exit codes: 0 success, 1 system error, 2 usage error, 3 not found, 7 partial result, 130/143/129 interrupted (SIGINT/SIGTERM/SIGHUP)
